title: Delayed Hydrogen-Induced Cracking: Fundamentals and Real-World Examples
abstract: Abstract Delayed hydrogen cracking represents a critical damage phenomenon in metallic materials, characterized by a temporal separation between hydrogen uptake and crack initiation. This time dependency often complicates failure analysis, as cracking may occur hours, days, or even years after manufacturing or commissioning. While hydrogen embrittlement has been extensively studied, the mechanisms governing delayed cracking are frequently discussed in isolation rather than as an integrated process. This paper presents a mechanistic framework for delayed hydrogen cracking by systematically linking hydrogen uptake, hydrogen configurations, stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution, and hydrogen-induced damage mechanisms. It is shown that the mere presence of hydrogen is insufficient to cause delayed cracking. Instead, the phenomenon arises from the ability of hydrogen to remain mobile or to be re-activated from initially benign configurations, followed by time-dependent redistribution toward regions of elevated mechanical stress and thus strain. Only when a critical local hydrogen concentration is reached do hydrogen-enhanced damage mechanisms such as hydrogen-enhanced decohesion and hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity become operative. The resulting fracture morphologies are discussed as the fractographic manifestation of these time-dependent processes rather than as indicators of a single dominant mechanism. Differences in fracture appearance across various material classes are addressed in this context. Finally, selected technical failure cases are presented to illustrate how hydrogen introduced during manufacturing or service can lead to delayed cracking under practical operating conditions. By integrating fundamental hydrogen–material interactions with real-world failure examples, this paper provides a comprehensive understanding of why hydrogen-induced cracking may occur long after hydrogen exposure and offers a structured basis for failure analysis and risk assessment of hydrogen-exposed components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hydrogen is widely regarded as a key energy carrier for achieving a climate-neutral industrial society. When produced from renewable energy sources, hydrogen enables the decarbonization of sectors that are difficult or impossible to electrify directly, such as primary steel production, chemical processing, large-scale energy storage, and long-distance transportation [ 1 ,  2 ]. As a result, hydrogen is increasingly introduced into existing and newly developed technical systems, ranging from pipelines, pressure vessels, compressors, and valves to turbines, fuel cells, and heat treatment facilities.

Consequently, a broad variety of engineering components are exposed to hydrogen during manufacturing, processing, storage, and service. In many applications, hydrogen is present at elevated pressures and temperatures or in combination with mechanical loading, which places stringent demands on the structural integrity and long-term reliability of materials. Metallic materials, particularly steels and high-strength alloys, play a central role in hydrogen technologies due to their favorable mechanical properties, manufacturability, and cost efficiency. At the same time, these materials are known to be susceptible to hydrogen-related degradation phenomena.

From a materials engineering perspective, hydrogen represents a unique challenge. Owing to its small atomic size and high mobility, hydrogen can enter metallic materials, diffuse through the lattice, interact with microstructural defects, and locally alter the mechanical behavior. These interactions may result in a pronounced loss of ductility, premature fracture, or time-dependent failure under stresses that would otherwise be considered safe. The risk is particularly critical for high-strength steels (> 800 MPa UTS), where even very small amounts of diffusible hydrogen can cause significant embrittlement [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ].

Importantly, the detrimental effects of hydrogen on metals are not a novel phenomenon introduced by modern hydrogen energy technologies. Hydrogen-related damage mechanisms have been known in engineering practice for decades. Classical examples include cathodic stress corrosion cracking in aqueous environments, hydrogen-induced cold cracking in weldments, and delayed fracture of high-strength fasteners and components. These failures often occur without previous warning signs (e. g., perceptible plastic deformation) and may develop hours, days, or even years after manufacturing or commissioning.

Among these damage mechanisms, hydrogen-induced delayed cracking represents a particularly critical and challenging failure mode. Cracks typically initiate and propagate under static or residual stresses long after hydrogen uptake has occurred, frequently in the absence of ongoing hydrogen exposure. The pronounced time dependency of delayed cracking complicates both failure analysis and lifetime prediction, as the underlying processes are governed by the interaction of hydrogen transport, microstructure, and local stress states.

This paper addresses the mechanisms of hydrogen-induced delayed cracking in metallic materials with a particular focus on the interaction between microstructure, hydrogen uptake, diffusion and stress state. The fundamentals of hydrogen behavior in metals are discussed first, including hydrogen configurations in metals and stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution. Building on these fundamentals, the underlying damage mechanisms and their fractographic manifestation in different material classes are described. Finally, selected technical failure cases are presented to demonstrate how the discussed mechanisms lead to delayed cracking in real engineering components, linking fundamental material behavior to practical failure analysis.

sections.heading: Hydrogen in Metals—Some Fundamentals
Hydrogen Configurations
paragraphs: This chapter establishes the first necessary condition for delayed hydrogen cracking by distinguishing between different hydrogen configurations in metals. In fact, the total hydrogen content is distributed between diffusible and trapped states (Fig.  1 ). This distinction is essential for understanding hydrogen-induced cracking and, in particular, the time-dependent nature of delayed cracking. While both hydrogen configurations may coexist within a component, their relevance for damage initiation differs fundamentally [ 8 ,  9 ]. Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of various hydrogen configurations in metals. Used with permission from [ 10 ]

sections.heading: Diffusible Hydrogen
paragraphs: Diffusible hydrogen refers to interstitially dissolved hydrogen atoms within the metal lattice. In this configuration, hydrogen is able to migrate through the material via diffusion. This process is strongly influenced by concentration gradients, stress gradients, and temperature. Due to its high mobility, diffusible hydrogen can rapidly redistribute within a component and locally accumulate in regions subjected to tensile stresses, such as crack tips, notches, thread roots, or microstructural heterogeneities [ 8 ,  9 ,  13 ,  14 ].

From a damage mechanistic perspective, diffusible hydrogen represents the most critical hydrogen fraction with respect to hydrogen-induced cracking [ 8 ,  9 ,  12 ]. It directly participates in stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution and enables the activation of embrittlement mechanisms such as Hydrogen-Enhanced Decohesion (HEDE) and Hydrogen-Enhanced Localized Plasticity (HELP). Consequently, the susceptibility of a material to delayed cracking primarily correlates with the amount of diffusible hydrogen rather than with the total hydrogen content [ 9 ,  15 ].

The mobility of diffusible hydrogen is strongly dependent on the crystallographic lattice structure. Body-centered cubic (bcc) metals, such as ferritic or martensitic steels, exhibit very high hydrogen diffusion coefficients, typically in the range of 10 −7  to 10 −9  cm 2 /s at room temperature, depending on microstructure and alloying [ 9 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. In contrast, face-centered cubic (fcc) materials, such as austenitic stainless steels and nickel-based alloys, show diffusion coefficients several orders of magnitude lower, commonly around 10 −12  cm 2 /s and even lower [ 9 ,  12 ,  19 ].

At the same time, hydrogen solubility differs significantly between bcc and fcc lattices. While bcc steels exhibit relatively low hydrogen solubility, fcc materials can dissolve substantially larger amounts of hydrogen without immediate embrittlement, Fig.  2  [ 9 ,  19 ]. Fig. 2 Temperature dependency of hydrogen diffusion and solubility in bcc and fcc lattice. Illustration based own research and literature data [ 11 ,  16 ,  60 ]

This combination of low solubility but high diffusivity renders bcc steels particularly susceptible to hydrogen-induced delayed cracking, as even small amounts of diffusible hydrogen can rapidly accumulate at stressed regions and reach critical local concentrations.

sections.heading: Trapped Hydrogen
paragraphs: In contrast to diffusible hydrogen, trapped hydrogen is bound to microstructural defects within the metal lattice. Typical trapping sites include dislocations, grain boundaries, phase interfaces, vacancies, non-metallic inclusions, precipitates, and voids [ 9 ,  20 ]. These defects provide energetically favorable sites for hydrogen, reducing its mobility and effectively immobilizing it to varying degrees.

Hydrogen traps are commonly classified according to their binding energy. Shallow traps, such as dislocations or low-angle grain boundaries, exhibit comparatively low trapping energies (typically below ~ 30 kJ/mol H) and may release hydrogen at moderate temperatures or under mechanical loading. Deep traps, such as interfaces to carbides, inclusions, or voids, exhibit significantly higher trapping energies (often exceeding ~ 50 kJ/mol H) and may retain hydrogen over long periods of time even at elevated temperature [ 21 ].

As long as hydrogen remains trapped, it does not actively participate in stress-assisted redistribution and therefore does not directly promote hydrogen-induced cracking. For this reason, trapped hydrogen is generally considered non-critical with respect to immediate embrittlement and delayed cracking [ 9 ,  20 ].

sections.heading: Activation and Release of Trapped Hydrogen
paragraphs: The relation between diffusible and trapped hydrogen is not static. If there are still unoccupied traps, diffusible hydrogen tends to fill these spaces, effectively lowering the amount of diffusible hydrogen. Trapped hydrogen, however, may become mobile if sufficient activation energy is supplied. While thermal activation is a well-known mechanism for hydrogen release from traps, mechanical loading and plastic deformation also play a decisive role. Plastic deformation alters the local defect structure and stress state, which may reduce trapping energies, generate new diffusion pathways, or enable dislocation-assisted hydrogen transport [ 15 ,  22 ,  23 ].

Once released, the previously trapped hydrogen contributes to the pool of diffusible hydrogen and may significantly increase the local hydrogen concentration in stressed regions. This mechanism is of importance for delayed cracking occurring long after hydrogen uptake has ceased. A component may initially contain a large fraction of hydrogen in trapped states without showing any signs of embrittlement. Over time, however, changes in stress state, temperature, or microstructure may activate trapped hydrogen, leading to a delayed increase in diffusible hydrogen concentration and subsequent cracking [ 15 ,  20 ].

Hydrogen-induced delayed cracking is therefore governed not by the total hydrogen content, but by the time-dependent availability of diffusible hydrogen. Components with a high total hydrogen content may remain intact if hydrogen is predominantly trapped, whereas components with comparatively low total hydrogen content may fail if a sufficient fraction is diffusible and able to accumulate locally.

This distinction is of central importance for both failure analysis and lifetime assessment. Without considering hydrogen mobility and trapping behavior, delayed cracking may appear unpredictably. In reality, it is governed by diffusion-controlled hydrogen redistribution and the gradual activation of diffusible hydrogen under service-relevant conditions.

Note: The distinction between diffusible and trapped hydrogen yields that thermal hydrogen analyses methods such as Thermal Desorption Mass Spectrometry (TDMS) must be performed at a specific temperature level. If the potential risk of hydrogen embrittlement is of interest, the analyzing temperature typically is in the range of 200 °C to 300 °C. Thus, only diffusible hydrogen as the responsible fraction for delayed cracking is analyzed. The trapped hydrogen, however, is analyzed in the range of 300 °C (shallow traps) up to 900 °C (deep traps). Finally, the total hydrogen may be assessed by performing melt analysis at a temperature above the sample’s melting temperature.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Redistribution and Local Hydrogen Accumulation
paragraphs: While the distinction between diffusible and trapped hydrogen explains the fundamental mobility of hydrogen in metals, it does not yet account for time-dependent nature of hydrogen-induced delayed cracking. In engineering components, failure is not governed by the “average hydrogen content” within in a component, but by the local hydrogen concentration in highly stressed regions. Experimental observations and numerical simulations consistently demonstrate that hydrogen-induced failures are controlled by hydrogen redistribution processes that are inherently diffusion-driven and stress-assisted [ 12 ,  23 ,  24 – 25 ].

sections.heading: Diffusion-Controlled Hydrogen Transport under Stress-Free Conditions
paragraphs: In the absence of mechanical loading, diffusible hydrogen migrates through the metal lattice via interstitial diffusion driven by concentration gradients—obeying the common laws of diffusion. This process tends toward homogenization of the hydrogen distribution within the material. The kinetics of diffusion are governed by lattice structure, temperature, and microstructure, with particularly high diffusion rates observed in body-centered cubic steels.

However, recent experimental and numerical studies have shown that purely concentration-driven diffusion alone is insufficient to explain the pronounced localization of hydrogen observed in hydrogen-induced failures. Instead, stress fields and microstructural constraints must be considered to realistically describe hydrogen transport in engineering components [ 24 ,  26 ].

sections.heading: Stress-Assisted Hydrogen Redistribution: The Gorsky Effect
paragraphs: The coupling between hydrogen diffusion and elastic stress fields represents a fundamental mechanism governing hydrogen redistribution in metals. This effect, originally described by Gorsky, is based on a reduction of the chemical potential of hydrogen in regions subjected to tensile hydrostatic stress [ 25 ].

Modern finite-element simulations and in situ experimental studies have confirmed that tensile stress gradients act as a strong driving force for hydrogen migration, leading to progressive hydrogen enrichment in elastically strained regions such as crack tips, notches, thread roots, weld roots, and zones of high residual stress [ 12 ,  15 ,  23 ,  27 ]. Importantly, this redistribution mechanism operates under purely elastic loading conditions and does not require plastic deformation.

Schematically, the local hydrogen accumulation within the elastic strain field of a notched tensile test sample is shown in Fig.  3 . For martensitic Q + T steels a local increase compared to the overall concentration within the unstressed lattice up to factor 5 was found [ 12 ]. Fig. 3 Schematic drawing of diffusion-controlled hydrogen accumulation in elastically strained regions. Note: For presentation purposes, the amount of hydrogen atoms is exaggerated

The stress-assisted redistribution of hydrogen is inherently time-dependent. Depending on hydrogen diffusivity, temperature, and component geometry, the time required to establish locally elevated and thus critical hydrogen concentrations may range from hours to several years. During this process, the local hydrogen concentration can increase continuously, even if the global hydrogen content remains constant or decreases due to effusion [ 23 ,  28 ].

sections.heading: Interaction of Stress Fields, Trapping, and De-Trapping
paragraphs: Hydrogen redistribution in real materials is further influenced by microstructural trapping effects. As hydrogen migrates under the influence of stress gradients, it may be temporarily immobilized at microstructural defects. Advanced modeling approaches and experimental studies have demonstrated that trapping does not suppress stress-driven redistribution, but rather delays it and introduces additional time dependency [ 26 ,  29 ].

Recent work has shown that changes in stress state—such as load application, cyclic loading, or residual stress redistribution—can promote hydrogen de-trapping even in the absence of temperature changes. This leads to a delayed release of hydrogen into the diffusible hydrogen pool and enhances local hydrogen enrichment in stressed regions [ 15 ,  30 ].

sections.heading: Time-Dependent Local Hydrogen Enrichment and Engineering Relevance
paragraphs: The gradual accumulation of hydrogen in stressed regions provides a mechanistic explanation for the often-delayed nature of hydrogen-induced cracking. A component may initially contain hydrogen at non-critical levels and withstands applied loads without any damage. Over time, however, stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution and de-trapping processes may locally increase the hydrogen concentration until a critical threshold is reached [ 27 ,  28 ].

This time dependency explains why hydrogen-induced failures often occur after a distinct delay between hydrogen uptake or load application and fracture. It also forms the physical basis for mechanical testing procedures such as slow strain rate testing (SSRT), which deliberately allow sufficient time for hydrogen redistribution during loading in order to quantify hydrogen-induced degradation under near-service conditions [ 13 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen-Induced Cracking—Damage Mechanisms
paragraphs: Hydrogen-induced delayed cracking occurs when stress-assisted redistribution of diffusible hydrogen has led to local critical hydrogen concentrations in the material. At this stage, hydrogen actively interacts with the lattice, defects, and dislocation structures, thereby reducing fracture resistance and enabling crack initiation and propagation under stresses that would otherwise be non-critical. The following sections summarize the dominant damage mechanisms relevant for hydrogen-induced delayed cracking.

sections.heading: Hydrogen-Enhanced Decohesion (HEDE)
paragraphs: The Hydrogen-Enhanced Decohesion (HEDE) mechanism attributes hydrogen-induced cracking to a reduction in atomic cohesion within the metallic lattice. Hydrogen accumulates at regions of high hydrostatic tensile stress, such as crack tips, grain boundaries, phase interfaces, or highly strained lattice regions. There, hydrogen weakens interatomic bonds and lowers the cohesive strength of the material, thereby reducing the energy required for crack initiation and propagation [ 8 ,  15 ,  31 ].

As a consequence, fracture may occur with little to no macroscopic plastic deformation. HEDE is commonly associated with brittle fracture modes such as cleavage or intergranular cracking, particularly in body-centered cubic steels with high strength levels. Importantly, HEDE does not require extensive plastic deformation and may operate under predominantly elastic loading conditions, which is highly relevant for delayed cracking in service [ 15 ,  32 ].

Recent atomistic simulations and fracture-mechanics-based approaches demonstrate that hydrogen-induced reductions in cohesive strength are sufficient to explain crack initiation at hydrogen-enriched regions, provided that a critical local hydrogen concentration is exceeded [ 31 ,  33 ]. HEDE is particularly relevant for high-strength body-centered cubic steels, where cleavage or intergranular fracture may occur under predominantly elastic loading conditions.

sections.heading: Hydrogen-Enhanced Localized Plasticity (HELP)
paragraphs: In contrast to HEDE, the Hydrogen-Enhanced Localized Plasticity (HELP) mechanism is based on the interaction of hydrogen with dislocation motion. Hydrogen reduces elastic interactions between dislocations and lattice obstacles, such as solute atoms or dense dislocation networks (“forest dislocations”), thereby facilitating dislocation glide at lower stresses [ 8 ,  34 ].

This enhanced dislocation mobility does not result in uniform plastic deformation, but rather promotes highly localized slip. The resulting strain localization leads to stress concentrations, micro-void formation, and premature crack initiation. HELP therefore accelerates damage evolution by intensifying local plasticity, even though the global stress–strain response may show only limited changes [ 30 ,  34 ,  35 ].

HELP is particularly relevant in materials where cleavage fracture is suppressed, such as face-centered cubic alloys. In such materials, hydrogen typically causes a reduction in ductility rather than a transition to brittle fracture. Nevertheless, HELP-induced localization may strongly interact with other mechanisms and contribute to delayed crack initiation under static loading [ 27 ,  32 ].

sections.heading: Interplay of HEDE and HELP
paragraphs: While HEDE and HELP are often discussed as competing mechanisms, experimental and numerical evidence increasingly indicates that hydrogen-induced cracking in engineering materials is best described by an interplay of both mechanisms, rather than by a single isolated process [ 15 ,  33 ,  36 ].

Localized plasticity promoted by HELP may facilitate hydrogen transport toward crack tips and interfaces, thereby enhancing local hydrogen concentrations. Once a critical concentration is reached, HEDE may dominate crack initiation and propagation. This synergistic interaction provides a robust explanation for the wide range of fracture morphologies observed in hydrogen-induced delayed cracking, including mixed brittle–ductile fracture modes.

sections.heading: Fractographic Characteristics of Hydrogen-Induced Fracture
paragraphs: Hydrogen-induced cracking manifests not only through mechanical property degradation but also through characteristic fracture morphologies that reflect the underlying damage mechanisms. Fractographic SEM analysis therefore represents a key tool in the investigation of hydrogen-related failures, as it provides direct insight into the local fracture processes and their interaction with microstructure and stress state.

As discussed in the previous chapter, hydrogen-induced cracking is governed primarily by the mechanisms of Hydrogen-Enhanced Decohesion (HEDE), Hydrogen-Enhanced Localized Plasticity (HELP), and their synergistic interaction. These mechanisms do not lead to a single, unique fracture appearance. Instead, they give rise to a spectrum of fracture morphologies, ranging from cleavage-like brittle fracture to highly localized ductile fracture, depending on material class, microstructure, hydrogen mobility, and local stress conditions.

From a fractographic perspective, hydrogen does not introduce entirely new fracture modes. Rather, it modifies existing fracture mechanisms, shifts their relative contribution, and promotes specific morphologies that would otherwise not occur under comparable loading conditions. As a result, hydrogen-induced fractures often exhibit mixed or atypical features, which may complicate failure interpretation if the hydrogen contribution is not explicitly considered.

The fracture appearance associated with hydrogen-induced cracking is strongly material-dependent. In high-strength quenched and tempered steels, hydrogen frequently promotes cleavage or quasi-cleavage fracture with limited macroscopic plastic deformation. In cast irons, hydrogen may interact with graphite morphologies and casting defects, leading to preferential crack initiation and propagation along microstructural heterogeneities. Austenitic stainless steels, which are generally resistant to cleavage fracture, typically exhibit ductile fracture morphologies with pronounced slip localization and micro-void coalescence, often accompanied by reduced ductility rather than brittle fracture. Nickel-base and copper alloys may show subtle hydrogen-induced modifications of otherwise ductile fracture surfaces, while high-strength cobalt–chromium alloys can exhibit hydrogen-assisted fracture features that combine localized plasticity with interfacial decohesion.

Importantly, the observed fracture morphology is not solely determined by the intrinsic susceptibility of the material, but also by the local hydrogen concentration at the time of fracture, which is governed by hydrogen redistribution and trapping phenomena. Consequently, identical materials may exhibit markedly different fracture appearances depending on hydrogen source, exposure history, and loading conditions. This further emphasizes that fractographic features must always be interpreted in conjunction with material state, service history, and hydrogen-related mechanisms.

sections.heading: Hydrogen-Induced Fracture Surfaces of Different Metals
paragraphs: For low alloyed carbon steel and Q + T steel the fractographic appearance is predominantly linked to the materials UTS.

The ductile normalized ferrite-pearlite microstructure (Fig.  4 a) exhibits less plastic deformation after hydrogen charging. This becomes evident by less deformed and rather frayed crests of the pearlite interfaces (Fig.  4 b). This pattern is predominantly caused by the HELP-mechanism. Fig. 4 Fracture appearance of unalloyed carbon Q + T steel C60 [ 12 ]. Left column: reference fractures without hydrogen charging.  a  Normalized ferrite-pearlite (680 MPa UTS),  c  Q + T martensite I (1300 MPa UTS),  e  Q + T martensite II (1520 MPa UTS). Right column: Hydrogen-induced fractures of the same materials.  b  Normalized ferrite-pearlite (0.87 ppm diff. hydrogen),  d  Q + T martensite I (1.15 ppm diff. hydrogen),  f  Q + T martensite II (1.78 ppm diff. hydrogen)

Without hydrogen charging Q + T martensite with an UTS of around 1000 to 1300 MPa exhibits a mainly ductile dimple fracture (Fig.  4 c), while the hydrogen-induced fracture has a very distinct structure that is referred to as transgranular “featherlike” pattern (Fig.  4 d). The specifics of this structure are still subject to scientific investigations. However, the most likely explanation is the interplay of HEDE (cleavage) and HELP (slipping) yields alternating crack propagation paths along the respective lattice planes.

Lastly, uncharged high-strength Q + T steel (> 1300 MPa UTS) exhibits a mixed fracture pattern with both intergranular cleavage and transgranular ductile dimple fracture (Fig.  4 e). On the hydrogen-charged sample, one might find the typical features of HE, referenced in nearly all of the relevant literature (Fig.  4 f). These include gaping grain boundaries, micro voids and “crow’s feet.” However, the most important feature remains the present of transgranular “featherlike” structures, although the overall fracture appearance might be dominated by intergranular cracking. At even higher UTS, the fraction of intergranular cracking will steadily increase.
Deviations of the described fracture pattern might occur by varying alloys, hydrogen content and applied mechanical load.

In Fig.  5  the fracture appearance of ferritic–austenitic duplex stainless steel (DSS) 1.4462 is compared. As to be expected, the uncharged sample (Fig.  5 a) exhibits a fully ductile dimple fracture. However, the charged sample (Fig.  5 b) is characterized by distinct features. Since the microstructure consists of roughly 50 % ferrite (α, bcc) and 50 % austenite (γ, fcc), one can find “lattice-specific” fracture patterns. The ferritic bcc phase exhibits the same “featherlike” structure that has been described above (interaction of HEDE + HELP). The austenitic fcc phase, however, appears to be brittle—which would contradict the fundamentals of metal physics. Upon closer inspection, one will find intersecting slip planes indicating a mechanism referred to as “planar slipping.” This finding is directly linked to the HELP-mechanism demonstrating the nature of localized plasticity. Fig. 5 Fracture appearance of duplex stainless steel 1.4462.  a  Uncharged reference fracture.  b  Hydrogen-induced fracture (17.2 ppm diff. hydrogen)

Similar findings are made for other fcc materials such as Ni- and Cu-base alloys (Figs.  6  and  7 ) or even CoCrNi alloys (Fig.  8 ). In all cases, the apparent brittle cleavage fracture is caused localized slipping triggered by the HELP mechanism. Fig. 6 Fracture appearance of Ni-base alloy IN 625.  a  Uncharged reference fracture.  b  Hydrogen-induced fracture (17.7 ppm diff. hydrogen) Fig. 7 Fracture appearance of Cu-base alloy CuNi14Al3Fe1.  a  Uncharged reference fracture.  b  Hydrogen-induced fracture (3.8 ppm diff. hydrogen) Fig. 8 Fracture appearance of Co41Cr16Ni15 superalloy.  a  Uncharged reference fracture.  b  Hydrogen-induced fracture (2.3 ppm diff. hydrogen)

Important note: Metastable austenitic stainless steels are at risk forming temperature- or strain-induced martensite. Due its bcc / bct lattice structure the presence of martensite yields the risk cleavage and thus HEDE might appear. This must be kept in mind when choosing austenitic stainless steel for hydrogen applications.

sections.heading: Delayed Hydrogen Cracking in Technical Applications
paragraphs: The preceding chapters have established the physical and metallurgical fundamentals governing hydrogen-induced delayed cracking. Hydrogen configuration, redistribution, and the associated damage mechanisms have been discussed as interacting processes that collectively determine the susceptibility of metallic materials to time-dependent failure. In particular, it has been shown that delayed cracking is controlled by the local availability of diffusible hydrogen, its stress-assisted redistribution, and the activation of hydrogen-assisted damage mechanisms such as HEDE and HELP.

While this mechanistic framework is essential for understanding hydrogen-induced cracking, it does not by itself convey how these processes manifest in real engineering components. In technical practice, delayed hydrogen cracking rarely presents itself as an isolated material phenomenon. Instead, it appears as an unexpected and often catastrophic failure of components that may have been in service for hours, months, or even years without any apparent indication of damage.

At this point, the connection between fundamental mechanisms and practical failure analysis becomes crucial. The fracture morphologies discussed in the previous chapter represent the material-specific manifestation of hydrogen-assisted damage mechanisms. However, the reliable identification of delayed hydrogen cracking in technical components requires additional context: the source of hydrogen, the processing history, the service environment, and the temporal evolution of stresses and hydrogen distribution.

The following chapter therefore focuses on technical failure cases of hydrogen-induced delayed cracking. Selected examples from industrial practice are presented to illustrate how manufacturing-related (“internal”) and service-related (“external”) hydrogen uptake can lead to delayed failure in different materials and component geometries. Each case combines information on hydrogen source, material condition, loading history, and fracture appearance, thereby linking the fundamental mechanisms discussed earlier to their practical consequences.

By correlating hydrogen uptake pathways with characteristic fracture morphologies and failure scenarios, this chapter aims to demonstrate why delayed hydrogen cracking remains a critical challenge in engineering practice and why its reliable assessment requires an integrated understanding of materials science, processing, and service conditions.

sections.heading: Sources of Hydrogen Update—Internal and External Hydrogen
paragraphs: When investigating hydrogen-induced failures—especially when it comes to defining remedial actions—the source of hydrogen uptake needs to be identified. Hydrogen may be introduced into a component either during manufacturing or acquired during service (Fig.  9 ). Both pathways can result in critical hydrogen contents long before macroscopic cracking becomes apparent. Fig. 9 Manufacturing-related sources of “internal” hydrogen and service-related sources of “external” hydrogen [based on [ 37 ,  38 ]]

sections.heading: Manufacturing-Related Hydrogen Uptake
paragraphs: Hydrogen uptake during manufacturing represents a particularly critical scenario, as affected components may enter service already containing a potentially damaging amount of hydrogen. In such cases, delayed cracking can occur without any further hydrogen exposure, solely driven by residual or applied stresses. Therefore, damage caused by hydrogen from manufacturing process is also referred to as “internal hydrogen embrittlement.”

As soon as components exhibiting internal hydrogen are stressed, diffusion-controlled local hydrogen accumulation is triggered. In most cases, subsequent delayed cracking occurs within a few minutes up to a few days.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from the Melt and Subsequent Effusion
paragraphs: During steelmaking and casting, hydrogen may dissolve in the molten metal due to its comparatively high solubility at elevated temperatures. Typical sources include moisture in charge materials, alloying additions, and furnace linings. Upon solidification, the solubility of hydrogen decreases rapidly, leading to effusion of a large fraction of the dissolved hydrogen. At room temperature, less than 1 ppm of hydrogen remains in the solidified material.

Figure  10  summarizes typical alloying elements of steel with their respective hydrogen contents as well as the temperature-dependent hydrogen solubility of iron. Fig. 10 Left: Hydrogen content of different alloying elements [[ 39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ], own investigations]. Right: Hydrogen solubility in liquid iron [based on [ 43 ]]

In most technical processing routes, subsequent thermal treatments such as hot rolling, forging, or annealing promote further hydrogen effusion, so that melt-derived hydrogen is often considered uncritical for hydrogen embrittlement. However, in large cross section components or in the presence of microstructural features such as voids, inclusions, or segregation zones, hydrogen may be retained locally. While this hydrogen is rarely responsible for classical delayed cracking, it may contribute to pre-damage phenomena, often referred to as “flakes”, or act as a background hydrogen reservoir that becomes relevant when combined with additional hydrogen uptake in later processing steps.

Bear in mind: Delayed hydrogen-induced failure is rarely caused by hydrogen from the melting process. Large castings may crack internally within a few hours or days of cooling (“flaking”). In most cases, these flakes act as pre-damaged internal areas that may initiate subsequent failure modes, such as fatigue.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from Welding Processes
paragraphs: Welding processes constitute another important source of manufacturing-related hydrogen. The fundamentals are quite similar to hydrogen in metal melts (c.f.  3.1.2 ), since welding also yields a partial melting of the material.

Hydrogen may be introduced through moisture in consumables, surface contamination, or the dissociation of hydrocarbons in the welding arc. Due to the high temperatures involved, hydrogen readily diffuses into the weld metal and the heat-affected zone.

In combination with residual stresses and locally hardened microstructures, hydrogen introduced during welding may lead to hydrogen-induced cold cracking only a very short time after completing the welding process. In some cases, however, cracking is delayed and occurs after hours or days.

When using modern electrodes and filler material, the risk of hydrogen uptake during welding is generally low, since manufacturers have established drying processes with subsequent hydrogen-free storage.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from Heat Treatment Processes
paragraphs: At typical carburizing temperatures of approximately 900 °C both hydrogen solubility and diffusion rates are high, enabling hydrogen to penetrate deeply into the component.

Although hydrogen effusion occurs during cooling and subsequent tempering, the relatively low tempering temperatures (around 180 °C) commonly applied after case hardening may be insufficient to fully remove diffusible hydrogen, especially in large components such as gears used in wind turbines. As a result, critical amounts of hydrogen may remain within the component and later contribute to delayed cracking under service stresses.

Figure  11  shows a schematic drawing of a broken drive shaft as well as results of fractographic failure analysis. Several of these failed drive shafts were detected while being prepared for shipping. The main manufacturing steps of the drive shaft include: Normalizing Forging Q + T heat treatment “Short term” case hardening in methane (CH 4 ) Tempering at 180 °C for 90 min Bend straightening to remove thermal distortion 100 % nondestructive testing (NDT) ➔ no failures were found Storage until ready to ship ➔ Several failures detected Fig. 11 Schematic drawing of the cracked drive shaft and fractographic SEM investigation. Used with permission from [ 44 ]

Fractographic investigations yielded the conclusion that the fractures were caused by hydrogen-induced delayed cracking (red frame). Typical features of hydrogen-induced cracking, such as featherlike structures and gaping grain boundaries are present. The forced fracture (green frame) exhibits a ductile dimple surface. Since all drive shafts had been NDT tested, it was excluded that pre-damaged components had been stored.

Further process analyses proved that the “short term” case hardening introduced around 3.5 ppm diffusible hydrogen into the drive shafts. However, subsequent tempering fully removed the diffusible hydrogen. The solution to this failure was found by applying additional hydrogen analyses after the bend straightening process. Due to the forced plastic deformation of the material, previously trapped hydrogen was re-activated to diffusible hydrogen. Since bend straightening introduces residual stress, this was the driving force for local hydrogen accumulation within zones of residual tensile stress. After a few days in the storage, critical levels of hydrogen were reached and delayed hydrogen cracking occurred.
The problem was permanently resolved by limiting the amount of allowed thermal distortion prior to bend straightening and by applying an additional tempering step after bend straightening.

Note: Hydrogen-induced cracking of surface hardened components often appears very similar to hardening / quenching cracks. In these cases, it is recommended to perform laboratory-based comparative fractures on hydrogen-charged samples taken from the failed component [ 38 ]. In the present case, hardening cracks could easily be excluded, since all cracks propagated radially, not axially.

Bear in mind: Delayed hydrogen-induced cracking due to heat treatment processes usually results in failure during cooling or within a few hours afterward. To reduce the risk of failure, subsequent tempering should be performed as soon as possible for an adequate length of time.

If trapped hydrogen is re-activated by plastic deformation, failure may occur considerably later. However, once this reactivation process has happened, hydrogen-induced cracking is usually observed within a few hours.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from Galvanic Coating Processes
paragraphs: Galvanic coating processes represent one of the most critical sources of manufacturing-related hydrogen. Hydrogen may already be introduced during preprocess surface preparation steps such as pickling and acid cleaning. If these processes are not adequately inhibited, significant hydrogen evolution occurs due to the cathodic partial reaction accompanying anodic metal dissolution.

In many cases galvanizers tend to increase the current density to speed up the deposition rate (linear correlation). However, increasing the current density also yields an increased hydrogen evolution, thus aggravating the risk of delayed hydrogen cracking.

Finally, dense and defect-free metallic coatings may impede hydrogen effusion after processing, effectively confining hydrogen within the substrate. In such cases, storage times between coating and commissioning may be insufficient to allow hydrogen to escape, resulting in components that are put into service with elevated diffusible hydrogen contents. In some cases, even additional tempering (around 180 °C to 200 °C) with the specific aim of removing hydrogen are not sufficient.

Particularly at risk are components with Cu-, Ni- and Zn-coating. By modifying the coating properties, the risk of delayed HE can be reduced. A commonly applied example is using ZnNi instead of pure Zn.

As an example, we included one of the best-known cases of delayed fracture—a galvanized screw (Fig.  12 ). This particular screw had been used for mounting hanging cupboards in a new kitchen. In the middle of the first night after the assembly, the owner of the kitchen was wakened by loud bang—just to find his new cupboards lying on the floor. Fig. 12 Delayed hydrogen-induced cracking on a galvanized screw

Failure analysis of the broken screw yielded that the primary fracture was caused by delayed hydrogen cracking (Fig.  12 , red frame). In this case, the fracture is predominantly intergranular with pronounced crow’s feet and in parts featherlike structure visible. The forced fracture (Fig.  12 , green frame) is characterized by a ductile dimpled fracture.

A more detailed look into the manufacturing process proved the galvanizing process (incl. pickling) to be the source of hydrogen intake. Subsequently, no tempering / effusion heat treatment was performed so that high amounts diffusible hydrogen remained within the screw—hindered from effusion due to a dense Zn-layer. As soon as the screw was stressed by mounting the cupboard, hydrogen diffused into the highest strain region—in this case the underhead area—and local hydrogen accumulation started. After a few hours, a critical local hydrogen concentration had been reached and the screw failed.

Bear in mind: Hydrogen-induced delayed cracking of galvanized components does not usually occur during or immediately after the coating process. However, once a hydrogen containing and galvanized component is subjected to mechanical loading, stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution may be activated even weeks or months later. Crack initiation and final failure then usually occur within a few hours after loading.

sections.heading: Service-Related Hydrogen Uptake
paragraphs: In contrast to manufacturing-related internal hydrogen, service-related hydrogen uptake occurs during component operation and may persist throughout the service life. Therefore, damage caused by hydrogen from service environment is also referred to as “external hydrogen embrittlement.”

In general, the delay between stressing a component and the occurrence of external hydrogen embrittlement tends to be longer compared to internal hydrogen embrittlement. This holds especially true, if there is only a temporary hydrogen source present—e.g., varying gas atmosphere, temporary corrosion or due to downtime. However, failures might occur significantly faster when external hydrogen is added to a component that already contains internal hydrogen.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from Corrosion—Cathodic Stress Corrosion
paragraphs: Corrosion processes in aqueous environments represent one of the most important service-related sources of hydrogen uptake in metallic materials. In contrast to internal hydrogen, hydrogen generated during corrosion may be introduced continuously or intermittently throughout the service life of a component. This time-dependent hydrogen ingress plays a decisive role in hydrogen-induced delayed cracking, particularly under static or residual stresses [ 45 ,  46 – 47 ].

From an electrochemical perspective, hydrogen uptake during corrosion is intrinsically linked to the cathodic partial reactions accompanying anodic metal dissolution. While corrosion is commonly regarded as a material loss phenomenon, it simultaneously constitutes an effective hydrogen charging mechanism.

The released electrons are consumed by the cathodic counter reaction, the nature of which depends on pH, electrochemical potential, and environmental composition. In many technical environments, hydrogen evolution represents the dominant cathodic process and thus a significant source of hydrogen. [ 46 ,  48 ].

During this reaction, atomic hydrogen is formed at the metal surface. While the majority of adsorbed hydrogen recombines to molecular hydrogen and desorbs, a fraction may enter the metal lattice as diffusible hydrogen. The absorption efficiency is strongly influenced by surface condition, alloy composition, temperature, and the presence of recombination poisons such as sulfur- or arsenic-containing species [ 49 ].

Although hydrogen evolution kinetics are generally slower than in acidic media, hydrogen uptake may still occur, especially under conditions of cathodic polarization or localized corrosion. Surface damage, coating defects, or galvanic coupling can significantly enhance hydrogen generation and absorption even in mildly alkaline environments [ 45 ,  49 ].

Hydrogen uptake from corrosion processes is strongly enhanced under cathodic polarization. This may occur unintentionally due to galvanic coupling between dissimilar metals or intentionally as part of corrosion protection strategies such as cathodic protection (e.g., on subsurface pipelines). Cathodic polarization facilitates the hydrogen evolution reaction, thus increasing the flux of atomic hydrogen at the metal surface. This phenomenon is well documented for high-strength steels exposed to cathodically protected environments, offshore structures, and pipelines [ 50 ,  51 ].

A key characteristic of hydrogen uptake from corrosion processes is its potential persistence over extended periods of time. Hydrogen may be introduced gradually, locally, and repeatedly, leading to a progressive increase in local hydrogen concentration in stressed regions. As a result, delayed cracking may occur after months or even years of service, even if the overall corrosion rate appears low.

Note: Within the literature hydrogen-induced damage associated with corrosion is referred to in different terms: Cathodic hydrogen embrittlement Cathodic stress corrosion cracking (cathodic SCC) Hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (HISCC) Hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC) under cathodic conditions

Despite terminological differences, all these phenomena share the same fundamental mechanism: hydrogen generation at the metal surface due to cathodic reactions, hydrogen absorption into the metal, stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution, and subsequent activation of hydrogen-induced damage mechanisms [ 46 ,  52 ].

The example below shows broken M64 nuts (metric thread, 64 mm diameter) from an offshore wind turbine. The nuts were manufactured according to DASt guideline 021 and connected the monopile (yellow tube in Fig.  13 , anchored in the seabed) to the transitions piece (gray tube in Fig.  13 , above sea level) via a flange. To prevent seawater from entering the flange during heavy swells, an inflatable seal had been installed on the outside of the flange. The nuts were hot dip galvanized to decrease the risk of corrosion even further. Finally, all nuts and bolts were covered with polymer cups filled to the brim with water repelling grease. Fig. 13 Broken nuts M64 (metric thread, 64 mm diameter) from an offshore wind turbine. Used with permission from [ 44 ]. Left: Flange at the connection of monopile (yellow) and transition piece (gray) with details of the nut and bolt assembly as well as the inflatable seal (red). Center: Fragment of a broken nut within the protective polymer cup. Significant water ingress. Right: several broken nuts after cleaning, exhibiting white rust

Shortly before the whole wind park (consisting of over 20 individual wind turbines) was scheduled to go on stream, several broken nuts were found during a routine check-up. Failures occurred in every single wind turbine amounting to a total of several hundred broken nuts. Upon retrieving the broken nuts, it was found that significant amounts of sea water had entered the assembly (Fig.  13 , center). Consequently, all nuts exhibited severe white rust (Fig.  13 , right-hand side).

Subsequent failure analyses yielded the conclusion that all nuts failed due to delayed hydrogen-induced cracking. Similar to our previous examples, the primary fracture (Fig.  14 , red frame) exhibits the specific features of hydrogen embrittlement, i.e., intergranular cracking with gaping grain boundaries, crow’s feet and transgranular featherlike structures. The forced fracture (green frame), however, consists of transgranular cleavage with small amount of ductile dimple fracture. Fig. 14 Broken nuts M64 (metric thread, 64 mm diameter) from an offshore wind turbine. Fracture surface and fractographic investigation. Used with permission from [ 44 ]

The cause of damage was found in a flawed sealing design. Seawater had entered via the flange due to an undersized inflatable seal. Since all nuts had been assembled on the bottom part of the flange, the seawater ran down the bolts and filled the polymer cups. Another important piece of the puzzle was found in the manufacturing process of the nuts. To ensure a proper fit all threads were cut after the nuts had been hot dip galvanized. Therefore, the bare threads did not have any advanced corrosion protection.
Between assembly of the flanges and detection of the failures, a period of 2.5 years had elapsed.

Since every single nut and bolt assembly required extensive on-site checking for cracks or water ingress it was decided that all nuts had to be replaced. The overall costs, including redesigning the seal, additional downtime of the wind park, material cost, etc., amounted to several million Euros.

Bear in mind: Delayed hydrogen-induced cracking due to corrosion processes has the potential to pose a significant risk over an extended time period. If severe corrosion is present, cracks may form within a few hours—particularly in high-strength steel. However, if corrosion rates are low or intermittent, or if protective measures such as coatings need to be overcome, delayed cracking may not occur for several years.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Uptake from the Gas Phase
paragraphs: Hydrogen uptake from the gaseous phase represents a distinct service-related hydrogen source that fundamentally differs from hydrogen introduction during manufacturing or corrosion processes discussed in the previous chapters. In technical applications involving high-pressure gaseous hydrogen, such as storage vessels, pipelines, valves, and compressor components, materials are deliberately selected to minimize hydrogen-related damage. As a consequence, austenitic stainless steels and other hydrogen-resistant alloys are predominantly used [ 32 ,  53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ].
This dissociation step requires a high activation energy of approximately 437 kJ mol −1  [ 59 ] and thus does not occur spontaneously under typical service conditions.

At moderate service temperatures, thermal activation alone is generally insufficient to overcome this energy barrier. Consequently, hydrogen dissociation can only proceed if the metal surface itself provides the necessary activation energy through catalytic processes. However, in real-world environments metallic surfaces are rarely pristine. Exposure to ambient air inevitably leads to the formation of a thin, naturally occurring oxide layer, which acts as an effective barrier against hydrogen dissociation and absorption.

Only under specific conditions—such as mechanical damage to the surface, wear, or exposure to strongly reducing atmospheres—locally oxide-free regions may form. Thus, the metal surface may catalytically dissociate molecular hydrogen, enabling the subsequent adsorption and absorption of atomic hydrogen into the lattice. The individual steps are as follows: a → b       Physical adsorption b → c       Chemical adsorption c → d       Catalytic dissociation d → e       Absorption f           Hydrogen trapping g           Surface recombination and desorption
A schematic illustration of this sequence is found in Fig.  15 . Fig. 15 Schematic illustration of hydrogen absorption from gaseous atmosphere [based on [ 9 ,  12 ]]

In addition to pressure and temperature, the composition of the hydrogen atmosphere has a significant impact on the uptake of hydrogen from the gaseous phase. Mixed gas atmospheres containing additional reactive species can significantly alter hydrogen uptake by promoting higher concentrations or inhibiting uptake.

Certain admixtures act as hydrogen uptake promoters. Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), for example, is known to suppress hydrogen recombination at the metal surface, thereby increasing the fraction of atomic hydrogen available for absorption. Even small concentrations of such species can significantly enhance hydrogen uptake rates, including in materials generally regarded as hydrogen-resistant [ 57 ].

Conversely, oxidizing species such as oxygen may act as hydrogen uptake inhibitors by stabilizing surface oxide layers and impeding hydrogen dissociation. This inhibiting effect is highly sensitive to the local surface condition and may be locally lost due to mechanical damage, wear, or chemical surface reactions during service [ 58 ].

Many materials used in high-pressure hydrogen service, including austenitic stainless steels as well as nickel- and copper-based alloys, exhibit a face-centered cubic (fcc) lattice structure. As discussed in the chapter on hydrogen configurations, fcc materials are characterized by very low hydrogen diffusion coefficients compared to body-centered cubic steels. As a result, even if hydrogen is absorbed from the gaseous phase, subsequent hydrogen transport and stress-assisted redistribution proceed slowly at ambient or slightly elevated temperatures. The time required for hydrogen to accumulate locally at highly stressed regions may therefore extend over exceptionally long periods, frequently far exceeding practical service lifetimes [ 53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ].

Hydrogen solubility increases with hydrogen partial pressure in accordance with Sieverts’ law, while hydrogen diffusion rates are strongly temperature-dependent. Therefore, only significantly elevated temperatures may sufficiently increase hydrogen diffusivity, eventually accelerating the redistribution phase to technically relevant time scales. Therefore, applications involving both high hydrogen pressure and elevated temperature represent a more critical scenario than exposure to high-pressure hydrogen at ambient temperature.

In practice, failures in (pressurized) gaseous hydrogen almost invariably involve additional contributing factors, including corrosion processes, cyclic loading, unfavorable stress states, or surface degradation that locally facilitates hydrogen entry. For failure analysis, it is therefore essential to consider not only hydrogen pressure but also the complete operating history, including temperature excursions, mechanical loading, surface condition, and the presence of promoting or inhibiting gas species.

Bear in mind: Delayed hydrogen-induced cracking caused solely by exposure to high-pressure gaseous hydrogen is rarely reported. In most cases, additional factors such as corrosion or fatigue contribute to failure.

Due to the limited hydrogen absorption and low hydrogen diffusion coefficients of commonly used fcc materials, hydrogen redistribution at ambient temperatures proceeds extremely slowly, resulting in characteristic time scales that typically exceed practical service lifetimes. Only at significantly elevated temperatures hydrogen diffusion may eventually become fast enough for delayed hydrogen-induced cracking to occur within technically relevant time frames. However, even in these cases, failures typically occur after years of service time rather than within day or weeks.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Hydrogen-induced delayed cracking represents a complex, time-dependent failure mode resulting from the interaction of hydrogen uptake, transport, microstructure, and stress state. Although hydrogen-related damage phenomena have been known in engineering practice for decades, their reliable assessment remains challenging due to the pronounced delay between hydrogen introduction and crack initiation.

This work has shown that delayed cracking is not governed by the total hydrogen content of a component, but by the local availability of diffusible hydrogen. Hydrogen may be introduced during manufacturing or service and may initially be present in trapped configurations without causing immediate damage. Over time, stress-assisted hydrogen redistribution, governed by diffusion kinetics and trapping behavior, can lead to a gradual increase in local hydrogen concentration in highly stressed regions.

The coupling between hydrogen diffusion and elastic stress fields, commonly referred to as the Gorsky effect, plays a central role in this process. Even in the absence of continued hydrogen exposure, stress gradients alone may drive hydrogen enrichment at critical locations such as crack tips, notches, and regions of high residual stress. Once a critical local hydrogen concentration is reached, hydrogen-assisted damage mechanisms become operative.

Hydrogen-induced cracking is controlled primarily by the mechanisms of Hydrogen-Enhanced Decohesion (HEDE), Hydrogen-Enhanced Localized Plasticity (HELP), and their interaction. These mechanisms do not lead to a single characteristic fracture mode, but rather to a spectrum of fracture morphologies that depend on material class, microstructure, hydrogen mobility, and local stress state. Fractographic analysis therefore provides essential insight into hydrogen-related failure processes, while also requiring careful interpretation in the context of hydrogen source and service history.

The presented framework demonstrates that delayed hydrogen cracking is a predictable consequence of diffusion-controlled and stress-assisted processes, rather than a random or sudden event. A mechanistic understanding of hydrogen uptake, redistribution, and damage mechanisms is therefore essential for reliable failure analysis, lifetime assessment, and the prevention of hydrogen-related failures in engineering components.
